newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German stars unlikely to shine at Book Fair.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German stars unlikely to shine at Book Fair.

text.p: Publishers hoping to find a new star author in the networking mayhem of next week's Frankfurt Book Fair can be reasonably sure of one thing -- he or she will not be German.

Although Germany's publishing industry ranks third in the world after Britain and China -- with more than 74,000 new titles produced last year -- German writers don't come close to dislodging Anglo-American blockbusters from bestseller lists, even on their home turf.
The latest German bestseller rankings, published weekly in the Spiegel magazine, show U.S. novelist John Grisham topping the list with a translation of "The Rainmaker"

Anglo-American, Spanish and Scandinavian titles crowd the rest of the top ten, with Norwegian author Jostein Gaarder occupying fifth and sixth place, while the lone German-language representative, Johannes Mario Simmel, comes in tenth.
As many as 2,500 German publishers are expected to join the 6,661 exhibitors turning up for the Frankfurt Book Fair this year, which runs from October 2-7.

The Fair, the central theme of which this year is Ireland, is the industry's premier annual event. Organisers say that a majority of the world's book deals are discussed, if not finalised, here each year.

But German publishers have to accept that, apart from Guenter Grass, the country's best known living writer, the only German novelist to achieve global success in recent years was Patrick Sueskind with his acclaimed novel "Perfume" (1985).

The problem has become a focus for debate in Germany, where publishers say they are keen as ever to promote German fiction but concede that most German novels -- often criticised as pompous and introspective -- lack popular appeal in a crowded English-language-dominated market.
"They write for their peers rather than the public, as though they were producing scientific tracts," said one publishing source, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"No publisher is going to subsidise them if they can get a really sure bet elsewhere," the source added.

Munich-based publishing group Carl Hanser Verlag, operating in the "literary" end of the fiction market and sole German publisher of Ireland's Nobel prizewinning poet Seamus Heaney, is bringing a small retinue of German writers to the Fair along with its established stars.
"Of course we are hoping for some exciting buys from abroad but we are very concerned to promote our German writers as well," said spokeswoman Susanne John.
John, along with other publishing executives, noted that much contemporary German writing was too sombre and its language too complex to be easily marketable abroad.
Many German writers, including Grass, are prone to reflections on abstractions, usually on the complex phenomenon of "Germany" in the late 20th century.

Overshadowed by weighty predecessors like Heinrich Boell and Thomas Mann, German writing also lacks the straight narrative tradition that has freed their U.S. and British peers to be more playful and contemporary.
"I think the joy in free narrative, simple story telling is much easier to find in the U.S. for example, than it is here," said John.

The young Sofia-born novelist Ilia Troyanov, published in German but translated into English, is viewed as an exception and will be among Hanser's "stars" for the Fair but experience has taught the group not to set its targets too high.

Norwegian bestseller "Sophie's World", originally discovered by Carl Hanser, has sold over a million copies in Germany, for example. "But with a German, if it's not Guenter Grass, to be honest we are happy with 10,000 (in sales)," John said.
"Without our big names, we could not get involved with young talent at all."

The German book traders' association is making a strong push this year to promote German writing and is to link up with the British Translators' Association to produce a newsletter for British publishers to alert them to new German titles.

German exports of book titles are estimated at a paltry 3.2 billion marks ($2.10 billion) annually -- and most of this is generated in German-speaking Switzerland and Austria -- compared with overall German book sales of 16.5 billion marks ($10.85 billion) in 1995.

"The problem we face is a linguistic one predominantly," said association spokesman Eugen Emmerling. "Plus the English speaking world already covers so many exotic themes and places that it is hard to find room for other things."

Every seventh book sold in Germany is a translation and threequarters of these are of U.S. or British origin, which shows that the Anglo-American influence on popular German tastes is "getting disproportionate," Emmerling said.

"The German public is simply very much impressed by things like Hollywood films and other aspects of U.S. culture and of course these big international firms also have a better marketing position," Emmerling said.
But Emmerling added that Germany's taste for international fiction revealed an open-mindedness not often seen in foreign markets. "It's a positive thing," he said. ($1=1.5206 Mark)
